trivia: One of the most famous magazine covers ever printed shows a refugee girl from my land, staring straight into the camera with piercing sea-green eyes. Nobody knew her name for 17 years, until the photographer tracked her down again in 2002.
reveal: Sharbat Gula, the 'Afghan Girl' on National Geographic's June 1985 cover, photographed by Steve McCurry
image_license: No free image: original photo is copyrighted; use an illustration

trivia: Travellers who visit me often say my people are among the most striking-looking in the world. Centuries at the crossroads of Asia have mixed many ethnic groups, so alongside dark eyes you'll meet green, blue and grey ones, and in some mountain valleys even blond or red hair.
reveal: Afghanistan's mix of Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara, Uzbek, Nuristani and other peoples

trivia: Every 1 January, Facebook floods with birthday alerts for my people. Decades of war left many without birth records, so when passports, visas and social media demanded a date, a huge number simply picked the easiest one to remember.
reveal: 1 January, the default birthday on many Afghan IDs and passports

trivia: When COVID-19 hit in 2020, an all-girls teenage robotics team in my land set out to build cheap ventilators. With electronics shops shut, they used an MIT design and parts scavenged from old Toyota Corollas, the most common car on my roads.
reveal: The Afghan Dreamers, an all-girls robotics team from Herat

trivia: My most common men's name is Mohammad, and my most common women's name is Fatima. Ranking even higher than Fatima is 'Bibi', a respectful word for 'lady' that many women carry as part of their name. Traditionally, most of my people didn't have a family name at all, only a first name.
reveal: Mohammad (men), Fatima (women), with the honorific Bibi ranking even higher

trivia: I'm one of the youngest countries on Earth. About 42% of my people are under 15, and half the population is younger than 18, while the world's median age is over 30.
reveal: Afghanistan, with a median age of about 17

trivia: In 2005 villagers in my mountains found a wounded American Navy SEAL, and one of them hid him in his home, refusing to hand him over to the fighters hunting him. He was obeying an old tribal code: anyone who asks you for refuge must be protected, even at the risk of your own life.
reveal: Mohammad Gulab, who sheltered US Navy SEAL Marcus Luttrell under Pashtunwali's code of nanawatai

trivia: My largest ethnic group has supplied most of my kings and rulers, and for centuries its name was used interchangeably with my own. Yet far more members of this group live across the border in my neighbour than inside my borders.
reveal: The Pashtuns, about three times as many of whom live in Pakistan

trivia: A bestselling novel set in my capital, Kabul, opens with a kite-fighting tournament. Boys coat their strings with crushed glass to slice rivals' kites out of the sky, while 'kite runners' sprint through the streets to catch the losers as they drift down.
reveal: The Kite Runner by Khaled Hosseini (2003)

trivia: In the 1860s, one of my kings invited classical musicians from India to his court and gave them homes on a single street of the old capital. For the next century that lane was the heart of my classical music, and many of my master musicians today trace their lineage back to those Indian families.
reveal: Kharabat, Kabul's old musicians' quarter, settled under Amir Sher Ali Khan

trivia: The sarod, a star of Indian classical concerts, grew out of my national instrument, the rubab. Musicians in India modified this short-necked, deep-bodied lute, carved from a single block of wood, into the instrument maestros play today.
reveal: The Afghan rubab, ancestor of the Indian sarod
image_author: Unnamed photographer, released into public domain by Metropolitan Museum of Art

trivia: In a remote mountain village, a photographer found a group of boys with a fashion subculture all their own. Every day, with no internet, they wear colourful surma eyeliner, henna-painted nails, embroidered clothes and rolled wool caps decorated with flowers and butterfly clips.
reveal: The surma boys photographed by Daniel Malikyar
image_license: No free image: original photo is copyrighted; use an illustration

trivia: My women have a secret weapon: the landay, a folk poem of just 22 syllables, nine in the first line and thirteen in the second. Passed around orally and often anonymously, landays can be tender, bawdy or savage, mocking cowardly men, unwanted marriages and old husbands.
reveal: The landay, a Pashto folk couplet

trivia: I'm one of the last places on Earth where street photographers still earned a living with the kamra-e-faoree, or 'instant camera': a handmade wooden box that's camera and darkroom in one. Customers sat on the pavement and walked away minutes later with a black-and-white portrait.
reveal: The kamra-e-faoree, the Afghan box camera

trivia: When my president Hamid Karzai stepped onto the world stage in 2001 in a striped silk chapan coat and a grey lambskin karakul cap, Gucci's designer Tom Ford called him 'the chicest man on the planet'. He later donated one of his signature coats to the British Museum.
reveal: Hamid Karzai's chapan coat and karakul cap
image_author: Paul Cruickshank and members of the OTI-sponsored Joint Agency Operations Center.

trivia: At the launch party for Sgt. Pepper's in 1967, John Lennon wore one of my embroidered sheepskin coats, fur inside and suede outside. The Beatles made them a hippie must-have, and demand grew so fast that my artisans couldn't keep up and smelly imitations flooded the market.
reveal: The Afghan coat (embroidered sheepskin pustin), much of it from Ghazni

trivia: My soft, rolled-brim wool cap looks like a sack until you roll it up to fit your head. It became world-famous on a guerrilla commander who wore it pushed far back on his head while fighting the Soviets and then the Taliban. Some say it descends from a hat worn by Alexander the Great's Macedonians.
reveal: The pakol, made famous by Ahmad Shah Massoud

trivia: My southern embroiderers stitch geometric patterns so tiny and dense, without tracing a single line first, that it's hard to tell the front of the cloth from the back. A single shirt-front can take three months, and a set of these linens is a must in every bride's trousseau.
reveal: Khamak, Kandahar's fine embroidery

trivia: Rumi, the 13th-century poet whose verses now fill Western bookshelves, wedding vows and Instagram captions, is traditionally said to have been born in my ancient city of Balkh, once so grand it was called the 'Mother of Cities'.
reveal: Rumi and Balkh, in northern Afghanistan

trivia: My most widely spoken language is so close to my western neighbour's that people chat across the border with ease. It is essentially one Persian language travelling under three names in three countries: Dari here, Farsi in Iran and Tajik in Tajikistan.
reveal: Dari, the Afghan name for Persian

trivia: Until 1896, one of my mountain regions was officially called the 'Land of the Infidels'. Its people worshipped their own gods, carved wooden statues of their ancestors and spoke languages that form a branch of their own on the language family tree. After a king conquered and converted them, he renamed the region 'Land of Light'.
reveal: Kafiristan, renamed Nuristan by Amir Abdur Rahman Khan

trivia: To welcome Nowruz, the spring new year, my families soak seven dried fruits and nuts, such as raisins, apricots, pistachios and almonds, in water for days. The result, Haft Mewa ('seven fruits'), is a sweet, syrupy bowl that tastes like spring arriving.
reveal: Haft Mewa, the Nowruz dried-fruit compote

trivia: When my new year arrives in March, wild red tulips burst across the hills around one northern city, and a 40-day 'Red Flower Festival' begins. Huge crowds pour in from across the country to gather around a blue-tiled shrine as a giant banner is raised.
reveal: Gul-e-Surkh, at the Blue Mosque in Mazar-i-Sharif

trivia: On Eid, my men put on their best clothes and head to the parks clutching hard-boiled, painted eggs for duels. Each player taps his egg against a rival's, and whoever's shell cracks first loses his egg to the winner.
reveal: Tokhm-jangi, Eid egg fighting

trivia: My national dish is a fragrant rice pilaf named after my capital, Kabul. It's crowned with sweet, caramelised strips of carrot, raisins and almonds, with tender lamb often hidden underneath.
reveal: Kabuli pulao (Qabili palaw)

trivia: The big, cream-coloured chickpeas in your chhole are called 'Kabuli chana' because they reached India through my capital, Kabul, around two centuries ago. India still uses the name, even though it now grows far more chickpeas than I do.
reveal: Kabuli chana, named after Kabul

trivia: Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire, conquered India but never stopped missing my melons. In his memoir he wrote that when a melon from his old capital reached him in India, he wept the whole time he was eating it. He asked to be buried back in my land, and he was.
reveal: Babur, buried in the Bagh-e Babur garden in Kabul

trivia: Bread is at almost every meal here, and you rarely have to walk far for it. Roadside vendors sit beside wheelbarrows and carts stacked high with long, ridged flatbreads fresh from the tandoor, selling a fresh one for about the price of a cup of tea.
reveal: Afghan naan sold from roadside carts in Kabul

trivia: One of my oldest dishes is cooked in a teapot. Cooks pack lamb, fat and lentils into rows of small clay teapots and leave them to simmer for hours beside the fire, so every diner gets a personal pot of stew to pour over their bread.
reveal: Chainaki, the teapot lamb stew

trivia: Shepherds and travellers here carry rock-hard balls of salted, dried yoghurt called qurut that keep for months without a fridge. Crushed and soaked in water, they turn back into a tangy sauce spooned over dumplings and stews.
reveal: Qurut, dried yoghurt balls

trivia: My national sport is like polo with a twist. Dozens of horsemen wrestle over a headless goat carcass, and whoever drags it clear and drops it into the scoring circle wins.
reveal: Buzkashi

trivia: My men's cricket team learned the game as refugees in camps across the border, where cricket was everywhere. Within a few decades they were beating England, Pakistan and Australia, and in 2024 they reached a T20 World Cup semi-final, sending crowds dancing into the streets back home.
reveal: Afghanistan's national cricket team, in the 2024 T20 World Cup semi-final

trivia: I competed in ten Olympics without a single medal. Then in 2008 a 21-year-old who had learned taekwondo in a refugee camp beat the reigning world champion to win bronze in Beijing. The president phoned to congratulate him, and the government gave him a house.
reveal: Rohullah Nikpai, taekwondo bronze at Beijing 2008

trivia: A long-haired, high-fashion dog breed carries my name. Bred to hunt in my mountains and deserts, it later became a glamorous show dog, and Pablo Picasso owned one called Kabul that appears in several of his paintings.
reveal: The Afghan Hound, and Picasso's dog Kabul
image_author: Museum of Veterinary Anatomy FMVZ USP / Wagner Souza e Silva

trivia: My highest mountains are home to a wild sheep with the longest horns of any sheep on Earth, spiralling outward to nearly two metres. It's named after the Venetian traveller who described it on his way across the Pamirs to China.
reveal: The Marco Polo sheep of the Wakhan and Pamirs

trivia: That pinch of hing (asafoetida) in your dal probably came from me. India imports over a thousand tonnes of it every year but never grew a single plant until 2020, and around 90 per cent of its imports came from my fields.
reveal: Hing (asafoetida), mostly from Afghanistan

trivia: My first national park, Band-e-Amir, is a chain of six lakes so intensely blue they look photoshopped. They aren't held back by man-made dams but by natural walls of mineral that built up over thousands of years.
reveal: Band-e-Amir National Park, Bamiyan

trivia: One of my southern deserts has a name that needs no translation: Dasht-e Margo, the 'Desert of Death'. It is a vast, empty sweep of sand, gravel and dunes in my far south-west, with almost no water and very few people.
reveal: Dasht-e Margo
image_author: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC

trivia: High above one of my river valleys, miners blast their way into the rock for emeralds so fine that experts compare them with Colombia's best. Strangely, the gems turn up only on the valley's eastern side, and nobody seems to know why.
reveal: The Panjshir Valley emerald mines

trivia: Two rival empires drew a thin finger of land onto my map so that their borders would never touch. At its tip I share a tiny border with China, and crossing it moves your clock forward 3.5 hours, the biggest jump at any land border in the world.
reveal: The Wakhan Corridor, created by Britain and Russia

trivia: My highest peak towers 7,492 metres above sea level on my far north-eastern border with Pakistan, deep in the Hindu Kush. It was first climbed in 1960 by a Japanese expedition.
reveal: Noshaq, Afghanistan's highest peak

trivia: In 2001 the giant Buddha statues of Bamiyan, carved into a cliff 1,500 years ago, were blown up. In 2015 a Chinese couple brought one back for two nights, projecting a 3D image of light into the empty niche while locals played music and danced below.
reveal: The Buddhas of Bamiyan

trivia: My most famous blue-tiled shrine is home to thousands of pure-white pigeons. Locals say the place is so holy that if a grey pigeon joins the flock, it turns white within 40 days.
reveal: The Blue Mosque (Shrine of Hazrat Ali), Mazar-i-Sharif

trivia: On a hill outside my capital stands a 150-room European-style palace built in the 1920s by a modernising king, with some of the country's first central heating. Civil war left it a bullet-riddled shell nicknamed the 'dirty sieve', but it was restored in time for my 100th Independence Day in 2019.
reveal: Darul Aman Palace, built by King Amanullah Khan

trivia: Hidden in a remote river gorge stands a 65-metre brick minaret built around 1190, so cut off that the outside world only saw it in 1957. It's the world's second-tallest brick minaret, and it's thought to have inspired the tallest one, Delhi's Qutub Minar.
reveal: The Minaret of Jam, Ghor province

trivia: My grandest old mosque runs its own tile workshop. Since the 1940s craftsmen there have cut, glazed and fired every replacement tile by hand, without machines, so the dazzling blue mosaics covering its walls are being remade piece by piece.
reveal: The Friday Mosque (Masjid-i Jami) of Herat

trivia: Before it reached the British Crown Jewels, the Koh-i-Noor diamond belonged to my Durrani kings for more than 60 years. In 1813 one of them, a king in exile, was pressured into handing it over to Maharaja Ranjit Singh of Punjab.
reveal: The Koh-i-Noor, surrendered by Shah Shuja Durrani to Ranjit Singh

trivia: I'm nicknamed the 'graveyard of empires'. The British Empire retreated from my capital in 1842, the Soviet Union pulled out in 1989 after a decade of war, and in 2021 the last American troops flew out after twenty years.
reveal: Afghanistan, the 'graveyard of empires'

trivia: In January 1842, about 16,000 soldiers and camp followers set out from my capital to retreat through snowy passes. A week later a single wounded British army doctor rode up to the walls of a fort on an exhausted pony. Asked where the army was, he is said to have replied: 'I am the army.'
reveal: Dr William Brydon, the 1842 retreat from Kabul
image_search_query: Remnants of an Army Elizabeth Butler

trivia: In 1996 the world's most wanted terrorist made my land his base, sheltered by its rulers while al-Qaeda plotted the 9/11 attacks. When American bombs pounded his mountain cave hideout in December 2001, he slipped across the snowy border into my neighbour, where he hid for almost ten years until US Navy SEALs found him in 2011.
reveal: Osama bin Laden, the Battle of Tora Bora

trivia: For 14 years, more than 20,000 pieces of 2,000-year-old gold jewellery lay hidden in a vault beneath my presidential palace. Only a handful of trusted 'key holders' knew, and they kept the secret through civil war and regime change until the treasure was revealed in 2003.
reveal: The Bactrian gold of Tillya Tepe

trivia: My current rulers began as an insurgent movement and swept back into power in 2021 as foreign troops left. Five years on, they still haven't been given my seat at the United Nations, and only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their government.
reveal: The Taliban's Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan

trivia: Your orange carrot has roots in me. The earliest written records of carrots grown as a crop come from my land over 1,000 years ago, and those first carrots were purple and yellow. Orange ones only appeared centuries later in the Netherlands.
reveal: The carrot, first cultivated in Afghanistan

trivia: Europe usually gets credit for inventing oil painting, but the oldest known oil paintings are mine. They are Buddhist murals in cliffside caves, painted around 650 AD with walnut and poppy-seed oil, centuries before Europe's masters.
reveal: The Bamiyan cave murals
image_author:
Painting: 5th century CE (2-Dimensional painting in the Public Domain)

Photographer: undetermined

trivia: Over 1,000 years ago, a scholar from one of my northern cities wrote that mental illness can have causes in both the body and the mind. He separated what we'd now call neurosis from psychosis and described treatments that resemble cognitive therapy, centuries before modern psychology.
reveal: Abu Zayd al-Balkhi, Sustenance of the Body and Soul

trivia: In 2010 an internal Pentagon memo predicted I could become 'the Saudi Arabia of lithium', the metal inside every phone and electric-car battery. Geologists estimated nearly a trillion dollars of untapped minerals under my soil.
reveal: Afghanistan's lithium and mineral reserves

trivia: Saffron, the world's most expensive spice, has become one of my priciest crops, with about 95% of it grown around Herat. In 2025 I exported 38 tonnes worth more than $67 million, and a Brussels taste institute has rated my saffron the world's best year after year.
reveal: Herat saffron

trivia: In 1964 Soviet engineers bored a tunnel through my mountains at nearly 3,400 metres, so high that drivers had to adjust their carburettors for the thin air. For almost a decade it was the highest road tunnel in the world, and it cut a three-day journey to about ten hours.
reveal: The Salang Tunnel

trivia: In 2023 my government ordered every taxi in the country to be repainted from yellow to bright turquoise. In my scorching south, some of these cabs carry a home-made air cooler strapped to the roof, piping cold air in through the window.
reveal: Afghanistan's taxis, repainted turquoise in 2023; the roof coolers are in Kandahar

trivia: Raisins, dried apricots, figs, almonds and pine nuts are among my biggest earners. In 2024 I exported about 159,000 tonnes of dried fruit worth $474 million, and India is one of the top buyers.
reveal: Afghan dried fruit exports

trivia: Despite deep poverty and international sanctions, my currency was the best-performing in the world in the third quarter of 2023, according to Bloomberg. It rose about 9 per cent against the dollar on the back of aid money, remittances and strict currency controls.
reveal: The afghani

trivia: For years I grew most of the world's opium. Then in 2022 my rulers banned the poppy, and within a year cultivation fell by about 95%, handing the title of world's biggest opium producer to Myanmar.
reveal: Afghanistan's opium poppy, banned by the Taliban in 2022

trivia: The souvenir travellers most often carry home from me is a hand-knotted rug, usually deep red and covered in a repeating octagon pattern nicknamed the 'elephant's foot'. Many are woven by Turkmen families who learned the craft from their grandmothers.
reveal: Afghan Turkmen rugs with the fil-pai (elephant's foot) motif

trivia: After 1979 some of my carpet weavers swapped flowers and birds for tanks, helicopters and Kalashnikovs. These 'war rugs' became collectors' items, and the British Museum has one in its collection.
reveal: Afghan war rugs

trivia: The precious blue of the Virgin Mary's robes in Renaissance paintings came from a stone mined in one of my remote valleys for more than 6,000 years, and it could cost more than gold. Today travellers take that same deep-blue stone home as rings, beads and pendants, one of my most popular souvenirs.
reveal: Lapis lazuli from Sar-e-Sang, Badakhshan

trivia: Visitors to one of my western cities love taking home bubbly, imperfect blue-green glass cups, still blown by hand the way one family has done for about 300 years. They now melt old bottles and broken windows instead of quartz, and they fear they may be the last glassblowers left in the country.
reveal: Herat blue glass
